Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041958/assets/164c90893a07ae9657e90b6f2b25e53c9c4927b1f4a076429ba0521a98377f24.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x-3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x-3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {e}^{x-3}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={e}^{x-3}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=3\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & ={e}^{3-3}+C \\ 2 & =1+C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={e}^{x-3}+1 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({e}^{x-3}+1) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({e}^{x-3}+1)}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041958/assets/141c6dd6c91841238298b86fac1063c76faeb7cd103e13d2723f6ac05ed58f50.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=1\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =\frac{8}{(0+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{16}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ v & =\pm \frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}} \\ (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}(x+2)^{3} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+2)^{3} & =12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=8,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+2)^{3}=12t+8.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{3} & =12t+8 \\ x+2 & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
v(x)=1+4{x}^{2}.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=1+4{x}^{2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1+4{x}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{1+(2x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡2x & =t+K \\ 2x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t+C) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2t+C)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x-2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = x^2 + e^{x-2} + C.
$$

Now, since $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2}+{e}^{2-2}+C \\ 8 & =4+1+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v = \sqrt{2\left(x^2 + e^{x-2} + 3\right)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x = 1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({1}^{2}+{e}^{1-2}+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(4+{e}^{-1})} \\  & ≈2.96\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\, \textrm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{2}{0+1}+K \\ 2 & =2+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{4}{x+1} \\ v & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x) > 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}} \\ \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int \sqrt{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1)^{3/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = \dfrac{3C_1}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+1)^{3/2} =3t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{3/2} & =3t+1 \\ x+1 & =(3t+1)^{2/3} \\ x & =(3t+1)^{2/3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$
